Radar Level Transmitter Calibration: Reference Height, Empty and Full Distance, Blocking Distance, Level Offset, False Echo Mapping and 4 to 20 mA Checks

A radar never needs a span test with weights or water columns, yet many radar loops still read wrong on the first day. The fix is almost always in the geometry you enter, the echo you trust and the checks you make against a manual dip.

Reference Point and Tank Height Empty and Full Distance Blocking Distance False Echo Mapping Level to mA Calculator

Radar level transmitter calibration means entering the right tank geometry, removing false echoes and proving the reading against a manual dip. Learn each setting, the order of work, verification points and a level to mA calculator.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn radar level transmitter calibration, from tank geometry and false echo mapping to level offset and 4 to 20 mA checks.

What Is Radar Level Transmitter Calibration?

Radar level transmitter calibration is the setup and verification of a radar gauge so that the distance it measures by microwave time of flight is turned into correct level and a correct 4 to 20 mA output. Because the sensor measures distance directly, the work is mainly entering the reference height, empty and full distances, blocking distance and offset, then checking the result against a manual dip or reference gauge.

Quick Answer
  • Level = empty distance E minus measured distance D plus offset
  • Empty distance is from the sensor reference point to the 0 % level
  • Full span F is from 0 % to 100 % level, kept clear of the antenna
  • False echo mapping should end about 0.5 m before the real level echo
  • Verify at 3 or more levels against a dip tape or gauge glass

If you are new to the principle, start with our page on the radar type level transmitter and come back here for the field setup. This article covers non contact radar, while guided wave radar follows a similar idea with a probe, as compared in guided wave radar vs non contact radar.

ICS Schneider Messtechnik notes that a radar can work perfectly in electrical terms and still show a wrong level because it follows a reflection from a nozzle, ladder or weld seam.

Does a Radar Level Transmitter Need Calibration?

A radar does not need a traditional zero and span calibration with a pressure source, because its distance reading comes from the time of flight of microwaves. What it does need is correct configuration, false echo handling and periodic verification against an independent level reference.

What You Do Not Need
  • No hand pump or calibrator for zero and span
  • No water column or weight test
  • No density compensation for liquids
  • No sensor trim for distance in normal use
What You Still Must Do
  • Enter the right reference height and tank geometry
  • Map false echoes from nozzles and internals
  • Verify level against a dip or gauge glass
  • Check 4 and 20 mA at the control system
Do You Know?

In the Micropilot M FMR230 and FMR231 function manual, Endress+Hauser defines empty calibration as the distance from the flange, which is the measurement reference point, down to the minimum level. Full calibration is the span from that minimum level to the maximum level.

Key Settings Before You Start

Reference Point

The point on the flange or thread from which every distance is measured.

Best for: Check in the manual for your antenna type
Geometry
Empty Distance E

Distance from the reference point to the 0 % level, often the tank bottom or a nozzle.

Best for: Sets the 4 mA point in level mode
Geometry
Full Span F

Distance from 0 % to 100 % level, kept clear of the antenna tip.

Best for: Sets the 20 mA point
Geometry
Blocking Distance

Zone below the antenna where echoes are ignored, also called near range.

Best for: Nozzle ringing and close structures
Filter
Level Offset

Constant added to level to match a manual dip or tank datum.

Best for: Final fine adjustment
Correction

Endress+Hauser advises keeping the end of the range at least 50 mm away from the antenna tip because of corrosion and build up. Its manual also describes a safety distance in front of the blocked zone, with a default of 0.1 m.

Low dielectric products return a weaker echo, so check the guidance in our article on dielectric constant in level measurement before you decide the span and antenna. The beam width also matters near walls, and our page on radar level antenna types explains horn, drop and planar choices.

Quick Tip

Measure real tank height with a dip tape from the reference point. Drawings rarely show the real nozzle height or a sump, and every millimetre of error goes into the level.

Radar Level Transmitter Calibration Steps

The order of work matters in radar level transmitter calibration, because echo mapping done before the geometry is right can hide the real level.

1
Save the Old Configuration
Export or upload the existing setup so you can go back if a mistake is made.
2
Check the Installation
Confirm nozzle size, antenna length, alignment and distance from walls, inlet and agitator.
3
Enter Units and Geometry
Set distance units, tank type, empty distance E and full span F.
4
Set Blocking Distance
Add a small near range to block nozzle ringing without hiding the top of the span.
5
Map False Echoes
With the tank empty or at a known low level, map up to 0.5 m before the real echo.
6
Compare With a Dip
Take a manual dip and enter a level offset if the reading differs.
7
Check the Output
Simulate 4, 12 and 20 mA and compare with the DCS or PLC display.
8
Verify at Several Levels
Record radar and dip readings at low, middle and high level as left.

VEGA advises in its field service tips that you export the current configuration file before making changes. It also states that its distance A and B settings define the 4 to 20 mA output, measured from the radar reference point to the 0 % and 100 % points.

Level L = E minus D + offset
Percent = L ÷ F × 100
Output mA = 4 + 16 × L ÷ F
Solved example
E = 10.000 m, F = 9.000 m
Measured distance D = 3.500 m
Dip shows 6.520 m, radar shows 6.500 m
Offset = 6.520 minus 6.500 = 0.020 m
L = 10 minus 3.5 + 0.02 = 6.520 m
Percent = 6.52 ÷ 9 × 100 = 72.4 %
mA = 4 + 16 × 6.52 ÷ 9 = 15.591 mA

In this radar level transmitter calibration example the radar read 20 mm low against the dip, so an offset of plus 0.020 m was entered. A constant error usually means a wrong reference height, while an error growing with level points to span or echo.

Result

How to Do False Echo Mapping

False echo mapping, also called interference echo suppression, records the fixed reflections from nozzles, ladders, heating coils and welds so the radar ignores them. Endress+Hauser states that the mapping range must end 0.5 m before the echo of the actual level, and that mapping is preferably done with an empty tank.

ICS Schneider warns that a suppression range that is too broad can hide a genuine high level. Keep the mapping as short as the problem allows, and read our guide on radar level transmitter false echo handling for echo curve examples.

Check DistanceCompare shown distance with the real distance to the surface
Choose RangeSet mapping to end about 0.5 m before the level echo
Record MapStart mapping only when the device shows no error
Move LevelFill or drain and confirm the reading follows the product
Save Echo CurveKeep a copy of the curve for future troubleshooting
Do You Know?

VEGA gives a simple field trick for multiple echoes on its echo curve. Freeze the curve, change the level, and the real level echo is the one closest to the sensor that moved position.

Myth: Radar never needs any field work.
Fact: It needs correct geometry, echo handling and verification even though no span test is done.
Myth: A bigger mapping range is always safer.
Fact: A long map can hide a real high level and cause an overfill.
Myth: If the mA loop is right, the level is right.
Fact: A perfect loop can still carry a wrong level from a false echo or wrong tank height.
Myth: Offset can fix any error.
Fact: Offset only fixes a constant error, not one that changes with level.

4 and 20 mA Output Checks and HART Tools

Once level is right, check the analogue signal with the loop test or current simulation function of the transmitter. A mismatch here is a scaling or wiring problem, and our instrument loop checking procedure shows how to test it end to end.

Endress+Hauser lists alarm currents of 3.6 mA for MIN and 22 mA for MAX on the HART version of this radar. Make sure the control system treats these values as faults and not as real empty or full levels, as explained in live zero and dead zero in 4 to 20 mA.

Most modern radars are set up with a HART handheld, a DTM in FDT software, a vendor app over Bluetooth or a local display. Whatever the tool, the HART protocol carries the same data, so save the report with every radar level transmitter calibration record.

Wet Test vs Dry Setup

A dry setup uses tank geometry, the echo curve and loop simulation without moving the level. A wet test moves the real level and compares the radar with a dip tape, a gauge glass or another reference at several points, much like a level transmitter 5 point calibration.

For tanks with overfill protection, the high level function may need its own proof test, as discussed in tank overfill protection under API 2350. Treat any radar level transmitter calibration on these tanks as a safety related job with a signed record.

  • Old configuration saved before changes
  • Reference point and tank height confirmed by dip tape
  • Blocking distance not covering the 100 % level
  • Mapping ends about 0.5 m before real level echo
  • Offset recorded with dip value and date
  • 4, 12 and 20 mA checked at the control system
  • Echo curve saved as left

Troubleshooting Radar Level Readings

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Level stuck while tank movesLocked on a false echoRemap with tank at known low level
Constant error at all levelsWrong reference heightMeasure tank height, adjust E or offset
Error grows with levelWrong span or tank shapeCheck F and linearisation table
Echo lost during fillingFoam or turbulenceMove away from inlet, use stilling well
Reads full when emptyNozzle ringing in near rangeIncrease blocking distance or longer antenna

Foam absorbs microwave energy and weakens the echo, as covered in why foam affects level sensors. In turbulent tanks a stilling well gives a calm surface, but the radar must then be set for pipe mode.

Quick Tip

When a radar reading goes bad after months of good service, look at the echo curve before changing any setting. Build up on the antenna, a new internal pipe or a changed product often explains the problem in minutes.

Antenna gain and beam angle decide how much energy hits walls and internals, and the basics of antenna gain and directivity make that easier to understand. For other faults, use our general level transmitter troubleshooting guide.

Radar Level Transmitter Calibration FAQ

How do you calibrate a radar level transmitter?

For radar level transmitter calibration, enter the reference height, empty distance and full span, blocking distance and a false echo map at a known low level. Then compare the reading with a manual dip and add an offset if needed.

Finish by checking the 4, 12 and 20 mA values at the control system. Record the as left level, the offset and the echo curve.

What is empty and full calibration in a radar level transmitter?

Empty calibration is the distance from the sensor reference point down to the 0 % level. Full calibration is the span from that 0 % level up to the 100 % level.

Together they tell the transmitter how to turn distance into level and current. If either value is wrong, every level reading and every alarm will be shifted.

What is blocking distance in a radar level transmitter?

Blocking distance is a zone just below the antenna where the radar ignores all echoes. It is used to hide ringing from the nozzle and strong reflections from structures close to the sensor.

Keep it as small as possible so it never covers the 100 % level. Some models add a safety distance below it to warn before the level gets too close.

Why does my radar level transmitter show the wrong level?

The most common causes are a wrong tank height, a false echo from a nozzle or internal, foam on the surface or build up on the antenna. A wrong offset from an old dip can also cause a constant error.

Look at the echo curve to see which echo the radar is tracking. Then check the geometry settings against a fresh dip before you change the mapping.

How often should a radar level transmitter be verified?

Many plants verify radar level at least once a year against a dip or gauge glass, and more often on overfill or custody tanks. The interval should follow your site procedure and past as found results.

Also verify after any change to the tank, nozzle, antenna or product. Save the echo curve each time for later comparison.

Can a radar level transmitter be calibrated without filling the tank?

Yes, a dry setup can be done with tank geometry, echo mapping and loop simulation while the level stays where it is. A single dip comparison at the current level confirms the offset.

A full wet check at several levels is still better when possible. It proves that span and tank shape settings are right across the whole range.

What We Learn Today

  • Radar level transmitter calibration is mainly entering reference point, empty distance, full span, blocking distance and offset, then checking a manual dip.
  • False echo mapping should be done at a known low level and end about half a metre before the real echo so a true high level stays visible.
  • Check 4, 12 and 20 mA plus alarm currents at the control system, and save the echo curve and configuration report as the as left record.
